name: EV Charge Point
tagline: A controlled socket that talks to the car before it ever energises the cable.
terminals: L / N / E supply from a dedicated RCBO
CP (control pilot) — the signalling line to the vehicle
PP (proximity pilot) — tells the unit what cable is plugged in
parts: Contactor inside the unit — energised only after the handshake
Control pilot circuit — sets the available current by PWM duty cycle
6 mA DC leakage detection — required because DC blinds a Type A RCD
PEN-loss (open-circuit neutral) protection on PME supplies
LED status ring — standby, charging, fault
Cable entry and gland at the bottom of the enclosure
safety: A charge point is fixed electrical equipment on a PME supply, so the protective earth arrangement matters as much as the cable size. Where the supply is TN-C-S the installation normally needs an earth electrode or a PEN-loss device that disconnects all poles including earth — the one place in a domestic installation where switching the earth conductor is permitted.

points.label: Enclosure (IP rated)
points.detail: Outdoor units are typically IP54 or better with a UV-stable case and a seal around the lid. The rating applies to the whole installation, not just the box: every cable entry has to be glanded or routed from below, or water will find the one hole you left.

points.label: LED status ring
points.detail: The ring is the unit's only user interface: steady for ready, pulsing while charging, red or amber for a fault. It reports the state the control pilot negotiated, so a ring that never leaves standby usually means the handshake failed rather than a supply problem.

points.label: Rating plate and display
points.detail: The rating is not the supply size — a 7.4 kW unit on a single-phase supply draws 32 A continuously for hours, which is why charge points are treated as a load with a unity diversity factor and get their own dedicated circuit rather than sharing a ring.

points.label: Type 2 connector
points.detail: The socket carries L, N and PE plus two thin signal pins: CP (control pilot) and PP (proximity pilot). CP is the one that matters — the car pulls it to a defined voltage to say it is present, and the unit then applies a 1 kHz PWM signal whose duty cycle tells the car how many amps it may draw.

points.label: Cable entry and gland
points.detail: The supply arrives at the bottom through a gland that maintains the enclosure rating, and the earth for the electrode (where one is fitted) comes in the same way. Nothing is energised until the pilot handshake completes, so the connector pins are dead while the lead is unplugged.
